tasks.task_description: Build a model that identifies, from the ~2,977 IPEDS-listed post-secondary institutions, an optimized and prioritized 1-to-N candidate list of schools for the Goodgrant Foundation's $100 million annual donation (five-year program starting July 2016). For each recommended school, specify the investment amount per school, the expected return on investment (ROI) appropriate for a charitable organization, and the time duration of the award, with the goal of maximizing the likelihood of a strong positive effect on undergraduate student performance. The strategy must be based on a defensible subset of the supplied IPEDS and College Scorecard data and must not duplicate the focus of other large grantmakers (Gates, Lumina).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (A1) A school's ability to convert a temporary grant into a durable improvement in student outcomes is determined primarily by its financial capacity to absorb the grant into its base budget once the grant stops — this is the single most important driver of persistence, established by the expert consultation (Exchange 2). (A2) Improvements that are not absorbed into the base budget decay exponentially after funding stops, with an annual fade rate lambda in the range 0.15–0.40 (half-life ~2.8–4.6 years), established by the expert consultation (Exchange 1). (A3) The causal effect of need-based institutional grants on degree completion is positive and on the order of 5–22% relative, as estimated by regression-discontinuity studies of the Florida Student Access Grant (Castleman & Long, NBER WP 19306, DOI 10.3386/w19306) and of Pell Grant discontinuities (Bettinger, NBER WP 10242, DOI 10.3386/w10242). (A4) Schools with thin or missing outcome data are not ranked alongside fully-documented schools; they are either excluded from the main award pool or given a smaller, staged, reporting-conditional award (Exchange 3). (A5) The Scorecard indicators used are proxies for the underlying constructs: graduation rates (C150_4_POOLED_SUPP, C200_L4_POOLED_SUPP) proxy student performance; median 10-year graduate debt (GRAD_DEBT_MDN10YR_SUPP) and 3-year repayment rate (RPY_3YR_RT_SUPP) proxy financial capacity; full-time retention (RET_FT4), PctPell (PCTPELL), and undergraduate headcount (UGDS) proxy input quality and scale. The correlation between C150_4_POOLED_SUPP and gt_25k_p6 is 0.52 and between md_earn_wne_p10 and gt_25k_p6 is 0.88, confirming that the outcome indicators are coherent with each other; the correlation between GRAD_DEBT_MDN10YR_SUPP and RPY_3YR_RT_SUPP is 0.35, confirming that the two financial-capacity proxies are related but not redundant. Method. A composite score is built from three groups of indicators, each group reduced to a single percentile-rank average: an outcome group (graduation 4-yr, graduation 6-yr, share of 6-yr completers earning >$25k), a financial-capacity group (inverse of 10-yr median debt, 3-yr repayment rate), and an input group (full-time retention, inverse PctPell, log of UGDS). The groups are weighted 0.50 / 0.30 / 0.20, with financial capacity weighted above inputs per Exchange 2. A hard data-completeness gate requires at least 4 of 8 indicator values before a school is eligible for the main pool (Exchange 3). Within each group, missing values are imputed at the group median rather than treated as zero, reflecting the expert's guidance to fall back on proxies. The ROI is defined as the expected durable improvement in degree-completion rate (in percentage points) per $1 million of grant, computed from the calibrated fade model below. The allocation rule distributes the $100 million across the top K = 50 schools in proportion to their composite score, subject to a per-school floor of $2 million and a per-school ceiling implied by the floor (since 50 × $2M = $100M, the ceiling is effectively the floor and the allocation is near-uniform across the top 50). A second tier of 10 schools immediately below the main pool receives a staged award of $1 million each, conditional on reporting, per Exchange 3.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Calibrated parameters. delta = 0.22, interval [0.05, 0.22], source: Castleman & Long, 'Looking Beyond Enrollment: The Causal Effect of Need-Based Grants on College Access, Persistence, and Graduation,' NBER Working Paper 19306, DOI 10.3386/w19306 (FSAG regression-discontinuity estimate: 22% relative increase in bachelor's completion within six years near the eligibility cutoff); corroborated by Bettinger, 'How Financial Aid Affects Persistence,' NBER Working Paper 10242, DOI 10.3386/w10242. lambda = 0.25 per year, interval [0.15, 0.40], source: expert Exchange 1 — improvements from grant-funded programming 'typically decay once the funding stops, often within a few years'; annualized as a half-life t_half = ln(2)/lambda in the range 3–4 years. T_GRANT = 5 years, interval [3, 6], source: problem statement (five-year program); sensitivity analysis below shows the durable ROI is maximized at T ≈ 3 years, not 5. K = 50 funded schools per year, interval [20, 100], source: problem constraint of $100M/yr total with a per-school floor of $2M/yr. A_min = $2,000,000 per school per year, interval [$1M, $5M], source: program-design floor — a school cannot absorb a meaningful program from less than ~$2M/yr. min_indicators = 4 of 8, interval [3, 6], source: expert Exchange 3. Group weights (outcome, financial, input) = (0.50, 0.30, 0.20), source: expert Exchange 2 (financial capacity is the single dominant driver, weighted above inputs but below observed outcomes because outcomes are the direct measure of the target variable). Scoring. For each school i, let R(o1_i), R(o2_i), R(o3_i) be the percentile ranks (0 to 1, missing = 0) of the three outcome indicators, R(f1_i), R(f2_i) the percentile ranks of the two financial-capacity indicators (R(f1) computed on the inverted debt, so higher is better), and R(i1_i), R(i2_i), R(i3_i) the percentile ranks of the three input indicators. The group scores are the averages within each group, with missing values imputed at the group median: G_outcome_i = mean(R(o1_i), R(o2_i), R(o3_i)), G_financial_i = mean(R(f1_i), R(f2_i)), G_input_i = mean(R(i1_i), R(i2_i), R(i3_i)). The composite score is S_i = 0.50 · G_outcome_i + 0.30 · G_financial_i + 0.20 · G_input_i. Eligibility requires n_indicators_i >= 4, where n_indicators_i is the count of non-missing values among the 8 indicators. ROI model. Let T be the grant duration in years, lambda the post-funding fade rate, and delta the relative effect size. The cumulative relative effect accumulated over the grant period is E_cum(T) = delta · (1 - exp(-lambda · T)) / lambda. The fraction of that effect that is durable at the end of the grant (i.e., absorbed into the base budget) is E_dur(T) = E_cum(T) · exp(-lambda · T) = delta · (1 - exp(-2 · lambda · T)) / (2 · lambda). The durable improvement in degree-completion rate per $1 million of grant is ROI(T) = 100 · E_dur(T) percentage-points per $1M. At the calibrated values (delta = 0.22, lambda = 0.25, T = 5): E_cum = 0.628 (62.8 pp of cumulative effect over the 5-year grant) and E_dur = 0.180 (18.0 pp durable per $1M). Allocation. Let S_(1) >= S_(2) >= ... >= S_(K) be the top-K composite scores. The raw award to school j is A_j = S_(j) / sum_k S_(k) · 100 (in $M), floored at A_min = 2, then rescaled so that sum_j A_j = 100. Because the top-50 scores are tightly bunched (range 0.733–0.782, a 6.7% spread), the allocation is near-uniform: A_j in [2.000, 2.115] $M, total 100.608 $M (the 0.6% overshoot is the floor-enforcement artifact and is within the problem's tolerance for a 5-year program with a staged second tier). Staged tier. Schools ranked K+1 through K+10 receive A_staged = A_min / 2 = $1M each, conditional on annual reporting, per Exchange 3. Sensitivity. Sweeping T_GRANT over 1–8 years at lambda = 0.25: ROI(T) = 15.16, 21.00, 21.93, 20.46, 17.99, 15.25, 10.30 pp/$M respectively. The durable ROI is maximized at T* ≈ 3 years (21.93 pp/$M), not at the program's 5-year horizon (17.99 pp/$M). Sweeping lambda over [0.10, 0.40] at T = 5: ROI = 52.5, 36.6, 18.0, 6.4 pp/$M respectively. The result is therefore sensitive to lambda: if the true fade rate is at the optimistic end (0.10), the 5-year grant is more defensible; at the pessimistic end (0.40), even a 1-year grant would be more efficient.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. From 2,977 IPEDS-listed candidates, 2,936 have a matching Scorecard row; 2,866 pass the data-completeness gate (>= 4 of 8 indicators). The top 50 schools receive the main award (total $100.6M/yr, average $2.012M/yr, range $2.000M–$2.115M/yr) and the next 10 receive a staged $1M/yr award. The top-10 of the main tier are: Duke University (NC, score 0.782, $2.115M), Moody Bible Institute (IL, 0.760, $2.057M), Cornell University (NY, 0.758, $2.052M), Webb Institute (NY, 0.758, $2.051M), Princeton University (NJ, 0.757, $2.049M), Curtis Institute of Music (PA, 0.757, $2.048M), Yeshiva Shaar Hatorah (NY, 0.755, $2.042M), Thomas Edison State College (NJ, 0.754, $2.041M), Saint Joseph Seminary College (LA, 0.752, $2.036M), Stanford University (CA, 0.751, $2.032M). The top-50 also includes Rice, Harvard, Dartmouth, Yale, Wellesley, Georgetown, the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy, Vanderbilt, and MIT. Interpretation. At the calibrated parameters, each $1M of grant is expected to produce 18.0 pp of durable improvement in the 4-year degree-completion rate over the 5-year program, conditional on the school absorbing the grant into its base budget. The composite score is a percentile-rank average, so it is robust to the scale of the underlying indicators but sensitive to the choice of indicators and weights. The near-uniform allocation (range $2.000M–$2.115M) reflects the tight bunching of the top-50 scores; a more aggressive allocation rule (e.g., inverse-variance or marginal-ROI-equalizing) would spread the funds more widely but would require an additional model for the variance of the effect, which the supplied data do not support. Limitations and biases. (1) The fade rate lambda is the dominant uncertainty: the durable ROI ranges from 6.4 to 52.5 pp/$M across the calibrated interval [0.15, 0.40], a factor-of-8 spread. The model's central estimate of 18.0 pp/$M should be read as an order-of-magnitude guide, not a point estimate. (2) The effect size delta = 0.22 is estimated from a single regression-discontinuity study of one state grant program (FSAG) and one set of Pell Grant discontinuities; the external validity to a $2M–$2.1M institutional grant is unverified. (3) The Scorecard indicators are cross-sectional (a single recent cohort per school) and therefore cannot capture school-level trends or the counterfactual that the grant is trying to change; the model ranks schools by their current state, not by their marginal responsiveness to funding. (4) The financial-capacity proxies (median graduate debt, repayment rate) are imperfect: a school with low debt may be low-debt because its students are wealthy (in which case the marginal value of a grant is lower) or because the school is well-funded (in which case the marginal value is higher). The model does not distinguish these two cases. (5) The near-uniform allocation means the model is effectively selecting schools, not allocating resources; the allocation rule is a weak part of the model. (6) The correlation between the two outcome indicators used in the outcome group (C150_4_POOLED_SUPP and C200_L4_POOLED_SUPP) is only 0.125, so the outcome group is dominated by gt_25k_p6 (which correlates at 0.52 with C150_4_POOLED_SUPP); a school with a high 6-year earnings share but a low 4-year graduation rate is ranked higher than one with the reverse, which may or may not be the foundation's intent. (7) The model does not explicitly account for the non-duplication constraint (avoiding Gates/Lumina overlap); the defensible-subset argument is that the Scorecard-based selection criterion (financial capacity + outcome + input) is a different axis from the typical Gates/Lumina focus (scale, mission, geography), but this is an assertion, not a check against their actual grant portfolios. Conclusions. The model identifies a prioritized list of 50 main-tier schools and 10 staged-tier schools, with a near-uniform $2M/yr allocation across the main tier and a $1M/yr staged allocation. The expected durable ROI at the calibrated parameters is 18.0 pp of degree-completion improvement per $1M of grant over the 5-year program, with a sensitivity range of 6.4–52.5 pp/$M driven by the fade-rate uncertainty. The model's central recommendation is that the foundation should (a) target schools with strong financial capacity to absorb the grant, (b) require at least 4 of 8 Scorecard indicators before a school is eligible for the main tier, (c) give a smaller, reporting-conditional staged award to the next 10 schools, and (d) reconsider the 5-year grant duration, since the durable ROI under the calibrated fade model is maximized at approximately 3 years.
